title: SLC6A6-Mediated Taurine Uptake Sustains Corneal Epithelial Stem/Progenitor Cell Function to Counteract Age-Related Dysfunction

sections.abstract:
This study aimed to elucidate the role of SLC6A6-mediated taurine transport in maintaining corneal limbal stem/progenitor cell (LSPC) function and its implications for age-associated corneal wound healing.

Corneal amino acid profiles from C57BL/6J mice were analyzed via liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS). SLC6A6 expression patterns were mapped using single-cell RNA sequencing, quantitative PCR, and immunofluorescence. Pharmacological inhibition of SLC6A6 with guanidinoethyl sulfonate (GES) was applied in corneal wound healing models and murine corneal epithelial stem/progenitor (TKE2) cells. Transcriptomic profiling, RNA/protein analyses, and functional assays were performed in GES-treated TKE2 cells. Aged mice with corneal epithelium scraping received topical taurine supplementation (25 mg/mL, 5 times/day), and the corneas were collected for immunofluorescence staining. Moreover, TKE2 cells were treated with GES along with the Notch1 agonist valproic acid (VPA), or they were treated with taurine along with the Notch1 inhibitor GSI-IX (DAPT).

The cornea exhibited high taurine concentrations, with its transporter SLC6A6 predominantly localized in LSPCs (limbal stem cells, transient amplifying cells, and basal cells) and displaying age-dependent expression patterns. SLC6A6 inhibition delayed corneal wound healing, triggered senescence pathway activation and pluripotency suppression, and downregulated stemness markers (BCAM, p63, KRT14, Wnt4) and proliferative markers (Ki67), which recapitulated key features of corneal aging. This functional decline was reversed through topical taurine supplementation. Moreover, VPA effectively reversed the inhibitory effect of GES, whereas DAPT attenuated the effect of taurine, indicating involvement of the Notch1 signaling pathway in taurine-induced LSPC maintenance.

SLC6A6-driven taurine uptake critically regulates LSPC homeostasis, presenting a therapeutic strategy for age-related corneal disorders.

Keywords: taurine, SLC6A6, stem/progenitor cell, corneal wound healing, Notch
sections.methods:
C57BL/6J mice (3, 11, and 24 months old) were obtained from Vital River Laboratory Animal Technology (Beijing, China). All animal experiments were performed in strict compliance with the ARVO Statement for the Use of Animals in Ophthalmic and Vision Research and were approved by the Ethics Committee of the Eye Institute of Shandong First Medical University.

Corneas of C57BL/6J mice were thawed at 4°C, and two corneas were mixed with 50 µL isotope internal standards and 1 mL of cold methanol/acetonitrile/aqueous solution (2:2:1, v/v). The homogenate was sonicated at low temperature (30 minutes/time, twice), followed by incubation at −20°C for 1 hour. The mixture was then centrifuged for 20 minutes (14,000 RCF, 4°C). The supernatant was dried in a vacuum centrifuge. For liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) analysis, the samples were redissolved in 100 µL acetonitrile/water (1:1, v/v), adequately vortexed, and then centrifuged (14,000 RCF, 4°C, 15 minutes). The supernatants were collected for continued analysis. LC-MS/MS analysis were performed using ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography (UHPLC, 1290 Infinity LC; Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA) coupled to a quadrupole ion trap instrument (QTRAP 6500+; Sciex, Framingham, MA, USA). In electrospray ionization (ESI) positive modes, the conditions were set as follows: source temperature, 500°C; ion source gas 1 (Gas1), 55; ion source gas 2 (Gas2), 50; curtain gas (CUR), 30; ion spray voltage floating (ISVF), 4500 V; and multiple reaction monitoring (MRM) mode detection, ion pair. Multiquant 3.0.2 software was used to extract chromatographic peak area and retention time. The metabolites were identified by utilizing the correct retention times of the standards.

To establish corneal wound healing models, mice were anesthetized by intraperitoneal injection of 0.6% pentobarbital sodium, followed by topical application of proparacaine hydrochloride eye drops. The corneal epithelium was mechanically removed using an electric handheld epithelial scraper (Alger Inc., Lago Vista, TX, USA). Ofloxacin ointment was then applied to prevent infection. The wound healing progression was observed by 0.25% fluorescein sodium staining and photographed with a slit-lamp microscope (Topcon, Tokyo, Japan). The staining area was measured by the ImageJ (National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD, USA).

Both female and male mice were used to study the effect of age on corneal wounding healing. Given that corneal diameter in mice is closely associated with age and sex, to investigate the correlation between SLC6A6 and age, the central 3-mm corneal epithelial area in 3- and 11-month-old female mice (with no significant difference in corneal diameter between the two age groups) was scraped. However, in male mice, the size of corneal epithelial ablation was adjusted according to individual corneal diameter (3 mm for 3-month-old mice, 3.25 mm for 11-month-old mice, and 3.5 mm for 24-month-old mice). Taurine eye drops (25 mg/mL, Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) were supplemented to aged male mice (3, 11, and 24 months old) five times daily after corneal abrasion. To investigate whether reduced SLC6A6 expression impacts corneal repair, the selective pharmacological inhibitor guanidinoethyl sulfonate (GES, HY-113329; MedChemExpress, Princeton, NJ, USA) was administered to deplete taurine in normal mice. 30 Then, 1% GES was added to water 7 days prior to corneal epithelial debridement. Subsequently, using 100-mM GES eye drops or PBS five times daily for 3 days post-wounding.

A murine corneal epithelial stem/progenitor cell line (TKE2) was kindly provided by Tetsuya Kawakita, MD, PhD, of Keio University (Tokyo, Japan). The TKE2 cell line has been utilized in corneal epithelial stem/progenitor cell function research. 31 , 32 The TKE2 cells were cultured in keratinocyte serum-free medium (KSFM) basal medium (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA), supplemented with human keratinocyte growth supplement (HKGS; Thermo Fisher Scientific) and recombinant human epidermal growth factor (5 ng/mL; R&D Systems, Minneapolis, MN, USA) at 37°C with 5% CO 2 . To suppress taurine utilization, the TKE2 cells were treated with GES at a concentration of 20 mM or 40 mM

The cultured TKE2 cells were seeded in 12-well plates (500 cells per well), and the TKE2 cells were then treated with GES (20 mM or 40 mM). After 7 days, the colony formation abilities were investigated by crystal violet staining solution (C0121, 100 mL; Beyotime, Shanghai, China). The number and the area of all colonies were determined using ImageJ.

To investigate the role of Notch signaling in GES-induced LSPC suppression, TKE2 cells were treated with GES (40 mM) along with the Notch1 agonist valproic acid (VPA, 50 µM, HY-10585A; MedChemExpress) for 7 days to analyze colony numbers and area. Furthermore, to assess the necessity of Notch1 signaling in taurine-induced LSPC maintenance, KSFM medium (containing high endogenous taurine) was diluted 1:3 with PBS to establish a taurine-deficient environment. Exogenous taurine (1 mM) was supplemented to the diluted medium along with the Notch1 inhibitor GSI-IX (DAPT, 25 µM, HY-13027; MedChemExpress) for 7 days. The colony formation abilities were investigated with the aforementioned methodology.

For corneal whole-mount immunofluorescence staining, corneas were carefully dissected and fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA, Biosharp Life Sciences, Guangzhou, China) at 4°C for 1 hour. Corneas were permeabilized and blocked overnight at 4°C in blocking buffer (PBS containing 0.3% Triton X-100 and 5% bovine serum albumin [BSA]), and then incubated with anti-SLC6A6 (26725-1-AP, Proteintech, Chicago, IL, USA) or anti-KRT14 (IY1383542, Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA) antibodies at 4°C overnight. The corneas were subsequently incubated with Invitrogen Alexa Fluor 647–labeled donkey anti-rabbit IgG antibody or Alexa Fluor 488–labeled donkey anti-mouse IgG antibody for 2 hours at room temperature. Finally, corneas were stained with 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) for 5 minutes at room temperature. The staining was observed and captured using a Leica microscope (Leica Microsystems, Wetzlar, Germany), and the fluorescence density was calculated using ImageJ.

For immunofluorescence staining, mouse corneas were collected at 60 hours after wounding and embedded in optimal cutting temperature compound (Sakura Finetek, Torrance, CA, USA). The sections (10 µm) were permeabilized with 0.1% Triton X-100 for 15 minutes, followed by blocking with 5% BSA for 1 hour at room temperature. Then, the sections were incubated with anti-SLC6A6 (26725-1-AP; Proteintech), anti-KRT14 (IY1383542; Invitrogen), anti-MKi67 (ab16667; Abcam, Cambridge, UK), anti-p63 (12143-1-AP; Proteintech), anti-BCAM (26528-1-AP; Proeintech), or anti-Notch1 (20687-1-AP; Proteintech) overnight at 4°C. Then, the sections were incubated with fluorescently labeled secondary antibodies for 2 hours at room temperature. Finally, the sections were stained with DAPI for 5 minutes at room temperature.

The human corneas of healthy subjects were obtained from the eye bank of the Qingdao eye hospital, and the research was approved by the Shandong Eye Institute Ethics Committee (No. [2025]31). The method of human corneal immunofluorescence staining was the same as that of mouse. All sections were observed and captured using an Echo Revolve microscope (ECHO Laboratories, Palo Alto, CA, USA).

TKE2 cells were seeded in 12-well plates at a density of 5 × 10 3 cells per well and cultured with or without GES (40 mM) for 72 hours. Subsequently, cells were harvested using TransZol-Up (TransGen Biotech, Beijing, China), and RNA sequencing was performed by APTBIO (Shanghai, China) using a NovaSeq 6000 Sequencing System (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA) and MGISEQ-T7 instrument (MGI Tech, Shenzhen, China). Differential expression analysis was conducted using the DESeq2 package, with differentially expressed genes (DEGs) defined as those with an absolute fold change > 1.5 and an adjusted P value ( P adj ) < 0.05. Finally, principal component analysis (PCA), volcano plots, Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway enrichment, and heatmaps were generated using tools from https://cloud.oebiotech.cn/ and http://www.bioinformatics.com.cn/ .

The corneal epithelia of normal mice were digested by Dispase II (D4693; Sigma-Aldrich) overnight at 4°C. Total RNA was extracted using a TransZol Up Plus RNA kit (TransGen Biotech) and then reverse transcribed into cDNA by HiScript III RT SuperMix Kit (R323-01; Vazyme, Nanjing, China). Quantitative PCR was performed with a ChamQ Universal SYBR qPCR Master Mix (Vazyme) on a 7500 Real-Time PCR System (Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA, USA). The primers used are listed in Supplementary Table S1 .

Total protein was extracted and applied to 10% Super-PAGE Bis-Tris Gel (LK303, Epizyme Biomedical Technology, Shanghai, China). Then, it was transferred to the polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) membrane (Merck Millipore, Darmstadt, Germany). The PVDF membranes were blocked by nonfat dry milk for 2 hours at room temperature and incubated with anti-GAPDH (60004-1-Ig; Proteintech), anti-KRT14, anti-p63, anti-BCAM, anti-β-actin (66009-1-Ig; Proteintech), or anti-Notch1 antibody in universal antibody diluent (Epizyme Biomedical Technology) overnight at 4°C. The next day, the membranes were incubated for 2 hours at room temperature with an horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-conjugated secondary antibody (SA00001-1; Proteintech). The signal was detected by an enhanced chemiluminescence (ECL) chemiluminescent system.

The raw single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data of normal mice and young/old mice were obtained from the Gene Expression Omnibus under accession numbers GSE158454 33 and GSE182419 . 34 Cells with more than 15% mitochondrial reads and <200 genes were excluded. The signature genes for further clustering each cell population were inferred through the study of Lin et al. 34 Raw scRNA-seq data for epidermis were obtained from the Gene Expression Omnibus under accession number GSE227782 . 35 Cells with more than 20% mitochondrial reads and <200 genes were excluded. The signature genes for further clustering each cell population were inferred through the study of Zhang et al. 35

Pseudotime analysis was performed on the corneal epithelial cell populations using the Monocle2 package in R (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). 36 Gene ordering was performed by genes that were differentially expressed across corneal epithelial cells. 34 Specifically, gene ordering was performed by identifying genes that were differentially expressed across clusters and were dispersed with a q -value threshold of less than 0.005. The architecture of the pseudotime trajectory was then visualized employing the DDRTree dimensionality reduction algorithm, with default parameter values selected for the algorithm.

Statistical analysis was performed using Prism 9 (GraphPad, Boston, MA, USA). The data are presented as mean ± SD. The Mann–Whitney U test was employed to compare two groups, and paired t -tests were utilized in western blot analysis. For multiple comparisons, one-way ANOVA was performed, followed by either the Tukey honestly significant difference test or Dunnett test. Differences between measurement variables were considered significant for P ≤ 0.05.
sections.results:
To characterize amino acid distribution in corneal tissue, the concentration of free amino acids in the cornea of C57BL/6J mice was quantified using LC-MS/MS. Taurine emerged as the most abundant amino acid, exceeding glutamine (second highest) and lysine (third) by a significant margin ( Fig. 1 A). In mammals, intracellular taurine levels depend on endogenous synthesis (mediated by cysteine sulfinate decarboxylase [CSAD]) and transporter-mediated uptake (via SLC6A6, SLC6A13, or SLC36A1) ( Fig. 1 B). 37 Therefore, we categorized the scRNA-seq data of corneas from healthy C57BL/6 mice obtained from the database GSE158454 33 ( Fig. 1 C), and the marker gene expression patterns are shown in Figure 1 D. The scRNA-seq of murine corneal subpopulations (epithelium, stroma, endothelium, conjunctiva, immune cells) revealed that Slc6a6 expression was markedly enriched in the corneal epithelium compared to other compartments ( Figs. 1 E, 1 F). Conversely, CSAD, the rate-limiting enzyme for taurine biosynthesis, showed minimal expression in the epithelium ( Figs. 1 E, 1 F). Moreover, quantitative PCR (qPCR) and immunofluorescence staining validation of corneal epithelium confirmed these findings, with SLC6A6 expression being highest in the epithelium ( Figs. 1 G, 1 H). These data suggest that corneal epithelial cells rely primarily on SLC6A6-mediated taurine uptake rather than biosynthesis.

Taurine abundance and Slc6a6 expression in the cornea. ( A ) Free amino acid concentrations in the corneas of healthy C57BL/6J mice ( n = 5). ( B ) Schematic of taurine transport and synthesis pathways. ( C ) UMAP visualization of corneal cell clusters in healthy C57BL/6 mice. ( D ) Dot plot displaying marker gene expression patterns. ( E , F ) Violin plots ( E ) and UMAP projections ( F ) showing expression levels of Slc6a6 , Csad , Slc6a13 , and Slc36a1 . ( G ) Key genes involved in taurine synthesis and transport in the corneal epithelium. ( H ) Immunofluorescence staining of SLC6A6 in C57BL/6J mouse corneas ( n = 4).

Given the reported association of SLC6A6 with human limbal stem cell holoclone formation, 38 we investigated its expression dynamics during corneal epithelial differentiation. The murine corneal epithelial cells were further stratified according to the marker gene expression patterns shown in Figure 2 B. The corneal epithelial cells were identified as distinct subpopulations: stem/progenitor cells (including limbal stem cells [LSCs]), transient amplifying cells 1/2 (TAC1/2), basal cells, wing cells, and terminally differentiated cells ( Fig. 2 A). Pseudotime trajectory analysis showed an inverse correlation between Slc6a6 expression and differentiation status ( Fig. 2 C). The violin plots showed that Slc6a6 expression was highest in LSCs, TACs, and basal cells, declining progressively with differentiation ( Fig. 2 D). Moreover, the immunofluorescence staining confirmed the Slc6a6 location in mice and human corneas ( Fig. 2 E). These findings position SLC6A6 as a key taurine transporter in corneal epithelial stem/progenitor populations.

Slc6a6 was predominantly expressed in corneal epithelial stem/progenitor cells. ( A ) UMAP plots of corneal epithelial cell subpopulations. LSC, limbal stem cells; TAC1/2, transient amplifying cells 1/2; Basal, basal cells; Wing, wing cells; Squam: squamous cells. ( B ) Dot plot of marker gene expression patterns. ( C ) Monocle pseudotime trajectory analysis colored by cell clusters ( left panel ) and feature plots of Krt14 , Muc4 , and Slc6a6 across pseudotime ( right panel ). ( D ) Violin plots of Krt14 and Slc6a6 expression in corneal epithelial cells. ( E ) The expression of Slc6a6 in the corneal epithelium of C57BL/6J mouse and human donor corneas.

To assess the conserved role of SLC6A6 in stem cells, we analyzed single-cell datasets from murine epidermis GSE227782 . 35 The murine epidermal cells were further stratified according to the marker gene expression patterns shown in Supplementary Figure S1 B. Similar to corneal findings, Slc6a6 expression was enriched in epidermal stem cells and diminished upon differentiation ( Supplementary Fig. S1 C). This conserved expression pattern across epithelial tissues underscores the potential role of SLC6A6 in maintaining stem cell function through taurine metabolism.

The level of taurine has been found to show an age-dependent decrease. 26 To investigate whether age also impaired the expression of Slc6a6 in the corneal epithelium, the corneal epithelial cells from 12-month-old (aged) and 3-month-old (young) mice were analyzed ( GSE182419 ). 34 Based on the lineage-specific markers shown in Figures 1 D and Figure 2 B, the corneal epithelial cells were categorized into eight clusters: LSCs, TAC1, TAC2, basal cells, wing cells, squamous cells, conjunctiva, and immune cells ( Fig. 3 A). Notably, Slc6a6 exhibited predominant expression in LSCs, TAC1, TAC2, and basal cells ( Fig. 2 D). By aggregating these four stem and progenitor-enriched populations, a marked reduction in both Krt14 and Slc6a6 expression was observed in aged mice compared to young controls ( Fig. 3 B). Immunofluorescence staining further confirmed that SLC6A6 levels were significantly diminished in the corneal epithelium of aged mice ( Fig. 3 C), consistent with the age-dependent decline in taurine levels in the cornea. 26

SLC6A6 decreased in the corneal epithelial stem/progenitor cells of aged mice. ( A ) UMAP plots of corneal epithelial cells from young and aged mice. ( B ) Violin plots of Krt14 and Slc6a6 expression in stem/progenitor cells. ( C ) The expression of SLC6A6 in the corneal epithelium of young and aged mice ( left panel , n = 4), and the fluorescence intensity was quantified by ImageJ ( right panel ). ( D , E ) Gene scoring analysis using genes related to stemness ( D ) and differentiation ( E ). ( F ) The corneal epithelium of young mice (3 months old, female) and aged mice (11 months old, female) was stained with fluorescein sodium at 0, 24, 48, and 60 hours ( left panel , n = 7) after wounding, and the corneal wound closure was presented as the percentage of the original wound ( right panel ). Data are shown as mean ± SD. ** P < 0.01, *** P < 0.001, **** P < 0.0001.

To investigate functional consequences, we evaluated stemness and differentiation potential using stemness- and differentiation-related genes. Aged LSPCs displayed significantly impaired stemness and reduced early differentiation capacity compared to their young counterparts ( Figs. 3 D, 3 E). Functional validation through corneal epithelial debridement revealed delayed wound healing in aged mice, consistent with the compromised regenerative capacity of their epithelial progenitor pool ( Fig. 3 F). These findings collectively demonstrate that Slc6a6 downregulation in corneal epithelial progenitors correlates with both taurine deficiency and age-related functional decline in tissue repair.

To investigate whether reduced Slc6a6 expression impacts corneal repair, corneal epithelial abrasion was performed on mice that received GES orally (1% GES in drinking water) or GES orally and topically (1% GES in drinking water and 100-mM GES eye drops). The results showed that oral treatment exerted an inhibitory effect on corneal epithelial wound repair within 48 hours, whereas it was more pronounced with the oral and topical GES treatment, with significant inhibition still observed at 60 hours ( Fig. 4 A). Additionally, no significant difference of epithelial wound repair was found in mice with GES topical treatment compared to the control group, indicating that the topical administration of GES eye drops did not exhibit noticeable cytotoxicity on the corneal epithelium ( Supplementary Fig. S2 ). To determine whether GES directly modulates corneal progenitor cell function, we assessed Slc6a6 levels in TKE2 cells by qPCR. Consistent with in vivo observations, TKE2 cells displayed high Slc6a6 expression, mirroring the expression pattern of corneal progenitor cells ( Supplementary Fig. S3 ). Furthermore, treatment of TKE2 cells with increasing concentrations of GES induced a dose-dependent reduction in both colony number ( Fig. 4 B) and size ( Fig. 4 C), underscoring the critical role of Slc6a6 in maintaining progenitor cell clonogenicity and proliferative capacity. Additionally, Csad siRNA was used to explore its impact on the function of LSPCs. Results showed that siRNA significantly reduced Csad expression in TKE2 cells but did not affect LSPC clone formation ( Supplementary Figs. S4 A– S4 C). This finding suggests that the LSPCs primarily rely on taurine uptake rather than intracellular synthesis to maintain their function.

GES impairs corneal wound healing and TKE2 cell colony formation. ( A ) The corneal epithelia of mice (3-month-old males) treated with oral GES, oral and topical GES, or control were stained with fluorescein sodium at 0, 24, 48, and 60 hours after wounding ( left panel ), and the corneal wound closure was presented as the percentage of the original wound ( right panel , n = 6). ( B ) Colony formation ( left panel ) and number ( right panel ) in GES-treated TKE2 cells. ( C ) Colony area ( left panel ) and quantitative analysis ( right panel ) in GES-treated TKE2 cells. Data are shown as mean ± SD. * P < 0.05, *** P < 0.001, **** P < 0.0001.

To investigate the role of SLC6A6-mediated taurine uptake in regulating stem cell functionality, we performed transcriptome sequencing on TKE2 cells treated with either PBS or GES. The PCA analysis showed the repeatability ( Fig. 5 A), and the volcano plot showed the DEGs of TKE2 cells treated with GES or CON group ( Fig. 5 B). KEGG analysis revealed that GES-treated cells exhibited upregulation of senescence-related pathways and downregulation of stem cell pluripotency pathways ( Figs. 5 C, 5 D). The expression levels of cellular senescence markers, such as Cdkn2a , Cdkn2b , Mapk12 , Rad9b , Igfbp3 , and Mdm2 , were significantly upregulated following GES treatment ( Figs. 5 D, 5 E), suggesting that taurine is essential for maintaining stem cell function. Moreover, the expression of genes associated with antioxidant and most osmoprotective-associated genes was significantly downregulated following GES treatment ( Supplementary Fig. S5 ), indicating that antagonizing taurine downregulates the antioxidant and osmoprotective capacities of cells. Given the impaired function of corneal stem/progenitor cells and delayed corneal wound healing in aging mice, we further analyzed markers associated with stemness, proliferation, and differentiation. The results showed that GES significantly reduced the expression of genes linked to corneal epithelial stemness, proliferation, and differentiation ( Fig. 5 F). qPCR validation confirmed marked downregulation of stemness- and proliferation-related genes, including Bcam , Ki67 , Wnt4 , Krt14 , and Krt15 ( Fig. 5 G). Additionally, protein-level assessments of BCAM, p63, and KRT14 revealed significant reductions following GES treatment ( Fig. 5 H). Collectively, these findings highlight the critical role of SLC6A6-mediated taurine uptake in sustaining the function of stem/progenitor cells.

Transcriptomic profiling of GES-treated TKE2 cells. ( A ) PCA analysis of TKE2 cells treated with GES versus control (CON) groups. ( B ) Volcano plot of DEGs. ( C ) KEGG pathway enrichment for downregulated and upregulated genes. ( D ) Heatmaps show the expression of genes involved in cellular senescence and signaling pathways regulating the pluripotency of stem cells. ( E ) The cellular senescence-related genes detected by quantitative PCR. ( F ) Heatmaps show the expression of genes involved in stemness, proliferation, and differentiation. ( G , H ) The genes related to stemness and proliferation were detected by qPCR ( G ) and western blot ( H ). Data are shown as mean ± SD. * P < 0.05, **** P < 0.0001.

Aged mice exhibited significantly reduced SLC6A6 expression in corneal epithelial stem/progenitor cells ( Figs. 3 B, 3 C). To determine whether age-related corneal epithelial dysfunction mirrors the stem cell impairments caused by inhibited taurine uptake, we assessed stemness- and proliferation-related genes during wound healing in young and aged mice. The aged mice showed markedly lower expression of Ki67, p63, and BCAM ( Fig. 6 A), indicating that SLC6A6-mediated taurine dysregulation is a potential contributor to stem cell dysfunction. To systematically evaluate concentration-dependent effects, the effect of taurine eye drops at concentrations of 0.5% and 2.5% was observed in a murine corneal epithelial debridement model. The results showed that 2.5% taurine eye drops significantly promoted corneal epithelial wound healing, whereas 0.5% taurine had no significant effect ( Supplementary Fig. S6 ). Furthermore, taurine eye drops were administered to aged mice following corneal epithelial scraping. The results showed that taurine supplementation significantly accelerated corneal epithelial wound healing in aged mice ( Fig. 6 B). Immunofluorescence staining further demonstrated restored expression of Ki67, p63, and BCAM in taurine-treated aged mice ( Fig. 6 C). To investigate the expression pattern of Slc6a6 , the expression of Slc6a6 in the corneal epithelium of mice of different ages was determined. The results showed a negative correlation between Slc6a6 expression and age ( Supplementary Fig. S7 A). To explore whether taurine could promote corneal epithelial wound healing in young and older mice, taurine was applied after epithelial debridement in 3- and 24-month-old male mice. Taurine was found to significantly enhance corneal epithelial wound healing in both age groups ( Supplementary Fig. S7 B).

Taurine promoted corneal wound healing in aged mice. ( A ) The expression of Ki67, p63, and BCAM in the corneal epithelium of young mice (3-month-old females) and aged mice (11-month-old females) ( n = 4). ( B ) The corneal epithelium of aged mice (11-month-old males) treated with or without taurine (Tau) was stained with fluorescein sodium at 0, 24, 48, and 60 hours ( left panel ) after wounding, and the corneal wound closure is presented as the percentage of the original wound ( right panel , n = 8). ( C ) The expression of Ki67, p63, and BCAM in the corneal epithelium of aged mice (11-month-old males) treated with or without taurine ( n = 4). Data are shown as mean ± SD. * P < 0.05, ** P < 0.01.

To elucidate the mechanism underlying GES, the signaling pathway in GES-treated TKE2 cells was analyzed. GSEA and KEGG pathway analyses revealed significant downregulation of the Notch signaling pathway upon inhibition of SLC6A6-mediated taurine uptake ( Figs. 7 A, 7 B). Further interrogation identified suppression of Notch1 , Hes1 , and Dll1 in GES-treated cells, which was validated by qPCR ( Figs. 7 C, 7 D). Notably, Notch1 is reported to play a pivotal role in corneal stem cell-mediated injury repair, and its inhibition severely impedes epithelial regeneration. 39 Western blotting confirmed that SLC6A6-mediated taurine uptake is essential for maintaining Notch1 expression in corneal epithelial stem/progenitor cells ( Fig. 7 E). To assess the necessity of Notch1 signaling in taurine-induced LSPC maintenance, the taurine-cultured TKE2 cells were treated with Notch1 inhibitor DAPT. As expected, taurine supplementation significantly increased the colony area of TKE2 cells, but this effect was attenuated by the addition of the DAPT ( Figs. 7 F, 7 G). Furthermore, to investigate the role of Notch1 in GES-induced LSPC suppression, the TKE2 cells were treated with GES in the presence of Notch1 agonist VPA. The results demonstrated that GES treatment significantly reduced the colony area of TKE2 cells, but the addition of VPA effectively reversed these effects ( Figs. 7 H, 7 I). These findings indicate the critical role of the Notch1 signaling pathway as a mediator of taurine-induced stem/progenitor cell maintenance. Importantly, taurine supplementation in aged mice significantly upregulated Notch1 expression in the corneal epithelium ( Fig. 7 J). These findings suggest that SLC6A6-dependent taurine transport modulates stem/progenitor cell functionality and tissue repair through regulation of the Notch1 signaling pathway.

SLC6A6-mediated taurine uptake regulated the Notch signaling pathway. ( A ) KEGG analysis of upregulated/downregulated pathways in GES-treated TKE2 cells. ( B ) GSEA enrichment of the Notch signaling pathway. ( C ) Heatmap of Notch-related genes. ( D , E ) Genes related to the Notch signaling pathway were detected by qPCR ( D ) and western blot ( E ). ( F , G ) Colony formation ( F ) and colony area ( G ) in Tau-treated TKE2 cells with or without Notch1 inhibitor DAPT. ( H , I ) Colony formation ( H ) and colony area ( I ) in GES-treated TKE2 cells with or without Notch1 agonist VPA. ( J ) The expression of Notch1 in the corneal epithelium of aged mice treated with or without taurine. Data are shown as mean ± SD. * P < 0.05, ** P < 0.01, *** P < 0.001, **** P < 0.0001.
sections.discussion:
Taurine, an essential physiological compound, plays a critical role in maintaining bodily functions. In this study, we analyzed the levels of 23 free amino acids in the cornea and identified that taurine as the most abundant. Moreover, we found that the taurine transport gene Slc6a6 is predominantly localized in LSPCs, with its expression significantly reduced in LSPCs of aged mice. Antagonizing Slc6a6 markedly decreases the number and size of cell colonies in vitro and inhibits the corneal wound healing in vivo. Antagonizing Slc6a6 induces cellular senescence and downregulates the pluripotency pathway and genes related to cell stemness, proliferation, and differentiation. Moreover, taurine uptake also regulated the Notch signaling pathway in LSPCs. In aged mice, supplementation with taurine accelerates the corneal wound healing by restores the function of stem cells by activation the Notch signaling pathway. These findings indicated the potential therapeutic effect of taurine in age-related corneal diseases.

Taurine levels are sustained through both endogenous synthesis and exogenous uptake. The enzyme CSAD governs endogenous taurine production, and the taurine transporter SLC6A6 facilitates its exogenous uptake. Although humans can synthesize taurine, endogenous production is limited, making dietary intake and other external sources indispensable for maintaining adequate systemic taurine concentrations. 37 Our transcriptomic and protein expression analyses indicate that SLC6A6 is the predominant taurine transporter expressed in the cornea, whereas the expression levels of other potential taurine transporters, such as Slc6a13 and Slc36a1, are extremely low. This suggests that SLC6A6 is the primary mediator of taurine uptake in corneal cells. SLC6A6-mediated transport is particularly vital for preserving intracellular taurine levels and supporting its physiological roles. SLC6A6 functions similarly across tissues by transporting taurine for cellular uptake and providing antioxidant effects by scavenging reactive oxygen species (ROS). 40 However, its expression levels and functional roles differ significantly in specific tissues. In the intestines and kidneys, it is mainly involved in taurine absorption and reabsorption. 41 , 42 In the cardiovascular system, it protects against vascular diseases. 43 , 44 SLC6A6 is highly expressed and positively correlated with CD8 + T-cell proliferation and function. 45 In macrophages, SLC6A6 expression increases during polarization to a pro-inflammatory phenotype. 46 These distinctions are closely related to the physiological characteristics and functional requirements of different tissues. Our investigation further revealed that SLC6A6 is predominantly expressed in LSPCs. Notably, SLC6A6 expression was significantly reduced in LSPCs of aged mice. Functional studies demonstrated that pharmacological blockade of SLC6A6 markedly diminished both the number and size of LSPC colonies, underscoring the essential role of the transporter in taurine uptake and its importance in modulating LSPC functionality. These findings highlight the dependence of LSPCs on exogenous taurine and suggest that age-related declines in SLC6A6 expression may contribute to reduced regenerative capacity in the aging cornea.

As age increases, the levels of taurine in the blood gradually decline. This decline is observed across multiple species, including mice, monkeys, and humans, and is associated with various aging-related physiological changes. Supplementation with taurine has been shown to extend lifespan and promote tissue regeneration. 21 Taurine is an essential substance in the human body and plays key roles in processes such as antioxidative stress, anti-inflammation, osmotic protection, and regeneration. 27 Research indicates that taurine protects the corneal epithelium against corneal alkali burns, which serves as a model of limbal stem cell deficiency (LSCD), by suppressing NLRP3 expression and reducing the secretion of IL-18 and IL-1β. 47 Another study reported that a combination of 0.5% taurine and 0.4% sodium hyaluronate (SH) significantly decreased ROS formation and DNA damage compared to treatment with 0.2% SH or 0.4% SH alone. 22 Such treatment further alleviates the symptoms of dry eye disease; therefore, taurine supplementation might also be beneficial for patients with LSCD or dry eye disease. The age-related decline in corneal wound healing in mice is multifactorial. In an aged mouse model, we observed that supplementation with taurine via eyedrops accelerated the repair of corneal epithelial injuries and restored the function of stem cells in aged mice, thereby promoting the treatment of epithelial injuries in aged subjects.

Nakatsukasa et al. 48 detected the levels of amino acids in human tears and found that taurine was the most abundant amino acid. Moreover, taurine in tears declines with age, 26 and its depletion impairs the antioxidant and osmoprotective functions of corneal epithelial cells, which are essential for wound healing. 22 We also found that the expression of genes associated with antioxidant defense and osmoprotection was significantly downregulated following GES treatment, indicating that antagonizing taurine downregulates the antioxidant and osmoprotective capacities of cells. Moreover, our study reveals that the expression of SLC6A6 also declines with age, coinciding with a slowdown in wound healing in aged mice. GES, an inhibitor of SLC6A6, has an inhibitory effect on corneal epithelial wound repair, indicating the crucial role of SLC6A6 in the wound healing process. Importantly, supplementation with taurine eyedrops restored the function of stem cells and significantly promoted corneal epithelial wound healing in young and aged mice. This indicates that the combined effect of reduced taurine availability and diminished SLC6A6 expression likely contributes to the impaired wound healing in aged mice. Although topical taurine restored LSPC function in aged mice, its clinical translation requires addressing ocular bioavailability challenges. Conventional eye drops exhibit low bioavailability (<5%) due to tear clearance and blinking, 49 yet the small molecular weight (125 Da) and hydrophilicity of taurine may enhance corneal penetration compared to larger molecules, as supported by its rapid systemic clearance ( T 1/2 = 1.0 ± 0.3 hour). 50 Although oral taurine (10 g/d for 6 months) shows no severe adverse effects in humans, 51 topical eye drops may cause transient irritation, allergic reactions, or blurred vision. Future priorities should include optimizing formulations to enhance corneal retention and conducting longitudinal safety studies to determine tolerance thresholds in aging populations with compromised epithelial barriers.

Studies have revealed that taurine regulates stem cell fate determination through multiple mechanisms. 52 , 53 In the neural system, taurine promotes the survival and neuronal differentiation of neural stem/progenitor cells by maintaining calcium homeostasis and activating the Shh signaling pathway, 54 , 55 with its neuroprotective effects potentially attributed to antioxidative properties that mitigate oxidative stress. 56 In somatic tissue regeneration, taurine supplementation enhances the population of Lgr5 + stem cells in intestinal epithelium and hair follicles, 21 , 57 , 58 while stabilizing chondrocyte phenotypes through suppression of type I collagen expression. 59 Moreover, taurine synergizes with retinoic acid to drive the differentiation of bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells into neuroretinal-like cells with therapeutic potential, offering novel strategies for cell-replacement therapy in retinal degeneration. 60 Similarly, we found that inhibition of taurine uptake significantly impairs the clonogenic potential of corneal progenitor cells, accompanied by downregulation of pluripotency pathways and activation of senescence signals.

The evolutionarily conserved Notch signaling pathway serves as a critical regulator of stem cell maintenance, differentiation, and tissue homeostasis. 61 In the cornea, immunohistochemical analyses have revealed strong Notch1 receptor expression at the basal layer of the limbal epithelium, the anatomical niche of LSPCs. This spatial localization suggests that Notch signaling plays a pivotal role in LSPC regulation, consistent with its known functions in controlling cell fate decisions through downstream targets including HES1, HES5, and HEY1. 62 – 64 Functional studies have demonstrated that Notch activation via Jagged-1 peptide accelerates corneal epithelial wound healing, and γ-secretase inhibitor (DAPT)-mediated Notch inhibition delays repair processes. Transgenic mice expressing the Notch intracellular domain (NICD) under the K14 promoter (K14-cre +/− /NICD + ) exhibit enhanced wound healing kinetics, with bromodeoxyuridine (BrdU) incorporation assays revealing doubled proliferative activity in corneal epithelium 6 to 12 hours post-injury compared to wild-type controls. 39 Conversely, Notch antisense (NAS) mice show impaired healing capacity. 65 Notably, NICD expression rescues differentiation defects in 14-3-3σ mutant corneal epithelial cells, underscoring the dual role of Notch in coordinating proliferation and differentiation. 66 In this study, we discovered that inhibiting the uptake of taurine by corneal epithelial stem/progenitor cells in vitro led to a significant downregulation of Notch1 expression. Conversely, during the corneal injury repair process in aged mice, the application of taurine could remarkably upregulate Notch1 expression. Therefore, taurine regulates the proliferation and differentiation of corneal epithelial stem/progenitor cells by upregulating the Notch1 signaling pathway, thereby facilitating the repair of corneal epithelial injuries in aged mice.

Autophagy modulation is crucial for promoting redox homeostasis and regulating the cell cycle, particularly under stress conditions such as radiation. Autophagic coupling with PAX6 has been shown to prevent hyperproliferation in limbal stem cells (LSCs). 67 Additionally, the Hippo/YAP signaling pathway plays a vital role in preserving the proliferative potential of LSCs. 68 YAP acts as a mechanosensitive regulator, where its nuclear localization is influenced by the stiffness of the limbal niche, which helps maintain stemness through TGFβ/SMAD2/3-mediated differentiation control. 69 This pathway also exhibits significant crosstalk with Wnt, Notch, and inflammatory pathways, positioning YAP as a key mediator in both regeneration and injury response. 70 , 71 Furthermore, anti-apoptotic signaling mediated by ABCB5 contributes to the quiescence and survival of LSCs, providing another target for enhancing LSC expansion and reprogramming. 72 The frizzled 7 (Fzd7) ligand–receptor interaction promotes LSC stemness and function, and therapeutic upregulation of Fzd7 signaling may facilitate the expansion of LSCs and reprogrammed LSC-like cells in culture. 73 Together, these strategies address both the depletion of stem cells and the deterioration of the niche associated with age-related limbal insufficiency, offering promising avenues for therapeutic intervention.

In summary, our study has identified SLC6A6-mediated taurine transport as being crucial for LSPC homeostasis, with significant clinical implications for age-related corneal disorders. The age-related decline in SLC6A6 serves as both a diagnostic biomarker and therapeutic target, with topical taurine supplementation showing promise in reversing corneal aging by restoring Notch1 signaling and stemness markers. These findings could shift treatment toward pharmacological management and offer new strategies for molecular diagnostics and combinatorial therapies.
